words.meaning: To represent or give an account of in words.
words.etymology: From Latin describere, from de- + scribere ‘to write’. The prefix and root together form the Latin verb behind English describe.
words.example: Can you describe the pattern you noticed?

words.meaning: Words written or engraved on a surface; also, a dedication in a book or artwork.
words.etymology: From Latin inscriptionem, from inscribere ‘to write on or in’, built from in- ‘in, on’ + scribere ‘to write’. The English noun came through Middle English.
words.example: The short inscription was carved above the doorway.

words.meaning: A written or typewritten composition or document, especially one distinguished from a printed copy.
words.etymology: From Latin manu scriptus, ‘written by hand’: manu (‘by hand’) + scriptus, the past participle of scribere (‘to write’). The script element is related to the Latin root; manu adds the idea of hand-writing.
words.example: She revised the manuscript before sending it to her editor.

words.meaning: A written, printed, or typed copy; especially, a typed copy of recorded or dictated material.
words.etymology: From Latin transcribere, ‘to copy or write again elsewhere’, from trans- ‘across’ + scribere ‘to write’; transcript is based on the Latin participle transcriptum.
words.relationship: Participle-based form: trans- + Latin scribere (through transcribere)
words.example: The interview transcript helped the team check its notes.

words.meaning: To carry or convey from one place to another.
words.etymology: From Latin transportare, ‘carry across’, from trans- ‘across’ + portare ‘to carry’.
words.example: Small boats transport supplies to the island.

words.meaning: To bring goods or services into a country from abroad.
words.etymology: From Latin importare, ‘bring in’, from an assimilated form of in- ‘in, into’ + portare ‘to carry’. The English verb also developed a separate sense ‘to signify’.
words.example: The shop imports tea from several regions.

words.meaning: To send or carry goods to another country for sale.
words.etymology: From Latin exportare, ‘carry out’, formed from ex- ‘out’ + portare ‘to carry’.
words.example: The farm exports fruit to neighboring countries.

words.meaning: Capable of being carried from place to place.
words.etymology: From French portable and Late Latin portabilis, from Latin portare ‘to carry’. The Latin verb is the shared root; English portable came through those later forms.
words.relationship: Root-related borrowing: from Latin portare through portabilis
words.example: A portable lamp made the reading nook easier to use.
